5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.
6. Support Profile
Aurelia raises a moderate number of tickets, typically 8 to 14 per quarter, and the distribution is unusual:
financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

result.question: What was the root cause of the BluePeak Electronics inventory synchronisation drift on 19 May 2026?
result.answer:
The drift was caused by **two independent faults** in the nightly stock batch pipeline:

- The scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset while the stock window should have been computed in IST, causing the feed to use an incorrect time zone.  
- A stale SKU‑mapping table left over from the March catalogue restructure was still being consulted, so some SKUs were resolved using outdated mapping data.  

Together these faults produced stock data that was up to 26 hours old, leading to the inventory synchronisation drift on 19 May 2026.

service_response.query: What was the root cause of the BluePeak Electronics inventory synchronisation drift on 19 May 2026?
service_response.answer:
The drift was caused by **two independent faults** in the nightly stock batch pipeline:

- The scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset while the stock window should have been computed in IST, causing the feed to use an incorrect time zone.  
- A stale SKU‑mapping table left over from the March catalogue restructure was still being consulted, so some SKUs were resolved using outdated mapping data.  

Together these faults produced stock data that was up to 26 hours old, leading to the inventory synchronisation drift on 19 May 2026.

2. Business Profile
Aurelia Home Decor designs and manufactures its own range of home furnishings. Unlike a reseller, Aurelia controls its entire catalogue, which means listing quality is consistently high and attribute disputes are rare.
The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.
Revenue is heavily seasonal. Roughly 38 percent of annual gross merchandise value is transacted between late September and early January, around the festive and wedding seasons. A second, smaller peak occurs in March. The account team plans catalogue campaigns, inventory buffers and support readiness around these two windows.

After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of

5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

The trade-off is that production lead times are long: a stock-out on a handwoven product line can take six to eight weeks to recover, so Aurelia manages inventory conservatively and reacts strongly to any platform issue that causes phantom stock or cancelled orders.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

2. Business Profile
GreenCart is the youngest account in the portfolio and the only one whose core product is perishable. Its business is built on recurring weekly subscription baskets rather than discrete purchases, which changes almost every operational assumption that applies to the other three sellers.
Subscription orders arrive in predictable batches tied to delivery slots. A delay that would be a minor inconvenience for a decor or footwear order is a total loss for fresh produce: if a same-day slot is missed, the goods are written off rather than re-delivered. GreenCart therefore treats fulfilment SLA as its primary metric and reacts to label or dispatch failures far more sharply than the other sellers.
The company is also small and capital-constrained. Cash-flow timing matters, which is why the January 2026
request for weekly settlement arrived before the account was technically ready for it, and why that request had to be handled as a documented policy exception rather than a routine change.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.
6. Support Profile
Aurelia raises a moderate number of tickets, typically 8 to 14 per quarter, and the distribution is unusual:
financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.
7. Current Watch Items
1. Settlement reconciliation hardening. The project opened after SC-001
is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.
2. Festive readiness. The account team must confirm inventory buffers and support cover before the late-September peak.
3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)

The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.

The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.

 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.

is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.

3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

5.1 Scenario SC-004 - Tax Invoice Mismatch (February 2026)
After an HSN revision, newly listed decorative lighting SKUs were not mapped to the 12 percent slab and defaulted to 18 percent. 1,240 invoices were issued at the wrong rate, producing a reconciliation mismatch of
INR 2,17,600. The mapping was corrected, credit notes were re-issued and a validation check was added to the listing workflow. The commercial decision and its rationale are recorded in the account decision record.
5.2 Scenario SC-001 - Settlement Shortfall (March 2026)
The settlement batch covering 5 to 9 March 2026 was short by INR 4,82,000. Engineering traced this to a deduplication key defect in the settlement ledger introduced during a schema migration, which double-deducted 1,914 reversal entries. The shortfall was credited on 14 March 2026. This is the highest-severity financial event on the account and remains the reference case for the reconciliation hardening project.
5.3 Scenario SC-010 - Checkout Regression (August 2026)
A platform-wide checkout release defect caused roughly 7 percent of cart-to-payment transitions to fail.
Aurelia was not the cause and was one of several affected sellers, but its festive pre-season traffic made the impact visible on the account. The release was rolled back within 34 minutes.

financial queries outnumber technical ones. Ritika Bansal raises tickets with precise order-level evidence attached, which shortens triage considerably. Rahul Sharma is the named support owner and handles the majority of the account's escalations.
 Settlement and payout queries: approximately 45 percent of ticket volume.
 Invoicing and tax queries: approximately 20 percent.
 Order and checkout failures: approximately 20 percent.
 Catalogue and listing questions: approximately 15 percent.

is still in progress; automated variance detection is live but the seller-facing variance statement is pending.

3. Tax mapping validation. The control added after SC-004 should be verified once the next HSN revision is published.

1. Purpose
This policy defines how long each category of platform information is retained, when it is disposed of, and how disposal is performed and evidenced.
It exists to balance two conflicting requirements: operational and legal needs to retain records, and the obligation not to retain information beyond its purpose.
2. Scope
Applies to all platform information: seller records, customer records, transaction records, tickets, incidents,
transcripts, runbooks, policies, access logs and diagnostic artefacts.
Applies to primary storage, backups, archives and analytical extracts.
3. Definitions
Term
Definition
Active period
Period during which a record is in routine operational use
Archive period
Period after the active period during which a record is retained but not routinely accessed
Disposal
Destruction or irreversible de-identification
Legal hold
Suspension of disposal for records relevant to a legal matter
De-identification
Removal or transformation of identifying fields so the record is no longer personal data

General operational instructions that describe how the company works are INTERNAL, because any employee may need them and they contain no seller-identifying commercial data. The Seller Onboarding

Engineering owns platform services and their reliability. not merely that a service returned to health.

IT owns identity, access administration, security monitoring and platform administration. The Platform
Administrator maintains user records, seller scope assignments and clearance levels, and leads security incident handling together with Engineering.

results.question: What went wrong in May?
results.answer:
## What went wrong in May

- **Root cause**: Two independent faults acted together in the nightly inventory batch pipeline.  
  1. The batch scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset while the stock window is calculated in Indian Standard Time (IST).  
  2. A legacy SKU‑mapping table left over from the March catalogue restructure was still consulted by the pipeline.  

- **Effect**: The combination caused the feed to publish stock data that was up to **26 hours old**, breaching the six‑hour freshness requirement.

- **Impact**:  
  - **18,400 SKUs** showed stale availability.  
  - **412 orders** were oversold, later refunded with priority handling.  
  - Listings appeared to have stock when the warehouses actually had zero, affecting both fulfilment centres (not uniformly).

- **Detection & timeline**:  
  - 19 May 08:15 IST – BluePeak reported receiving orders for items shown as in stock.  
  - 19 May 09:10 IST – Support confirmed the 26‑hour data staleness.  
  - 19 May 10:15 IST – Seller disabled the affected listings, stopping new oversells within ~20 minutes.  
  - 19 May 13:40 IST – Scheduler timezone defect identified.  
  - 19 May 16:20 IST – Stale SKU‑mapping table identified as the second factor.  
  - 20 May 09:00 IST – Scheduler pinned to **Asia/Kolkata** and stale mapping removed.  
  - 21 May 11:30 IST – SKU mapping rebuilt and full resynchronisation executed; listings re‑enabled at 15:00 IST.  
  - 23 May 12:10 IST – All 412 oversold orders refunded.

- **Underlying issues**:  
  - No freshness metric existed, so monitoring only reported job completion, not data currency.  
  - A permissive fallback (legacy mapping) hid the problem.  
  - The six‑hour freshness requirement was not enforced by any control.  

These faults and missing controls together caused the May incident.

service_response.query: What went wrong in May?
service_response.answer:
## What went wrong in May

- **Root cause**: Two independent faults acted together in the nightly inventory batch pipeline.  
  1. The batch scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset while the stock window is calculated in Indian Standard Time (IST).  
  2. A legacy SKU‑mapping table left over from the March catalogue restructure was still consulted by the pipeline.  

- **Effect**: The combination caused the feed to publish stock data that was up to **26 hours old**, breaching the six‑hour freshness requirement.

- **Impact**:  
  - **18,400 SKUs** showed stale availability.  
  - **412 orders** were oversold, later refunded with priority handling.  
  - Listings appeared to have stock when the warehouses actually had zero, affecting both fulfilment centres (not uniformly).

- **Detection & timeline**:  
  - 19 May 08:15 IST – BluePeak reported receiving orders for items shown as in stock.  
  - 19 May 09:10 IST – Support confirmed the 26‑hour data staleness.  
  - 19 May 10:15 IST – Seller disabled the affected listings, stopping new oversells within ~20 minutes.  
  - 19 May 13:40 IST – Scheduler timezone defect identified.  
  - 19 May 16:20 IST – Stale SKU‑mapping table identified as the second factor.  
  - 20 May 09:00 IST – Scheduler pinned to **Asia/Kolkata** and stale mapping removed.  
  - 21 May 11:30 IST – SKU mapping rebuilt and full resynchronisation executed; listings re‑enabled at 15:00 IST.  
  - 23 May 12:10 IST – All 412 oversold orders refunded.

- **Underlying issues**:  
  - No freshness metric existed, so monitoring only reported job completion, not data currency.  
  - A permissive fallback (legacy mapping) hid the problem.  
  - The six‑hour freshness requirement was not enforced by any control.  

These faults and missing controls together caused the May incident.

service_response.answer:
## What went wrong in May

- **Root cause**: Two independent faults acted together in the nightly inventory batch pipeline.  
  1. The batch scheduler applied a fixed UTC offset while the stock window is calculated in Indian Standard Time (IST).  
  2. A legacy SKU‑mapping table left over from the March catalogue restructure was still consulted by the pipeline.  

- **Effect**: The combination caused the feed to publish stock data that was up to **26 hours old**, breaching the six‑hour freshness requirement.

- **Impact**:  
  - **18,400 SKUs** showed stale availability.  
  - **412 orders** were oversold, later refunded with priority handling.  
  - Listings appeared to have stock when the warehouses actually had zero, affecting both fulfilment centres (not uniformly).

- **Detection & timeline**:  
  - 19 May 08:15 IST – BluePeak reported receiving orders for items shown as in stock.  
  - 19 May 09:10 IST – Support confirmed the 26‑hour data staleness.  
  - 19 May 10:15 IST – Seller disabled the affected listings, stopping new oversells within ~20 minutes.  
  - 19 May 13:40 IST – Scheduler timezone defect identified.  
  - 19 May 16:20 IST – Stale SKU‑mapping table identified as the second factor.  
  - 20 May 09:00 IST – Scheduler pinned to **Asia/Kolkata** and stale mapping removed.  
  - 21 May 11:30 IST – SKU mapping rebuilt and full resynchronisation executed; listings re‑enabled at 15:00 IST.  
  - 23 May 12:10 IST – All 412 oversold orders refunded.

- **Underlying issues**:  
  - No freshness metric existed, so monitoring only reported job completion, not data currency.  
  - A permissive fallback (legacy mapping) hid the problem.  
  - The six‑hour freshness requirement was not enforced by any control.  

These faults and missing controls together caused the May incident.

2. Business Profile
GreenCart is the youngest account in the portfolio and the only one whose core product is perishable. Its business is built on recurring weekly subscription baskets rather than discrete purchases, which changes almost every operational assumption that applies to the other three sellers.
Subscription orders arrive in predictable batches tied to delivery slots. A delay that would be a minor inconvenience for a decor or footwear order is a total loss for fresh produce: if a same-day slot is missed, the goods are written off rather than re-delivered. GreenCart therefore treats fulfilment SLA as its primary metric and reacts to label or dispatch failures far more sharply than the other sellers.
The company is also small and capital-constrained. Cash-flow timing matters, which is why the January 2026
request for weekly settlement arrived before the account was technically ready for it, and why that request had to be handled as a documented policy exception rather than a routine change.

which is the component involved in the September 2026 duplication event.
 Catalogue: managed in Shopify and mirrored to the platform.
The connector reduced GreenCart's integration effort but adds a translation layer. Two of the three scenarios on this account involve behaviour at the boundary between the connector and a platform service rather than a defect in GreenCart's own systems.

February 2026 had been issued at an 18 percent tax rate rather than 12 percent. Support raised the ticket the same day and confirmed the pattern across 1,240 invoices.
The cause was a mapping gap rather than a calculation defect. Following an HSN revision, the 12 percent slab applied to a subset of decorative lighting products. Existing SKUs were remapped as part of the revision, but SKUs created after the revision were assigned the category default, which remained 18 percent.
